scenario: Person whose entire community was killed or displaced and who grieves something the world has moved on from.
prompt: I go online and people are posting about their weekends. Last week someone I follow was upset about a restaurant that got their order wrong. I sat with that for a while. In my village there are no people left who remember it the way it was. I remember it. I remember the market on Thursdays and the smell of the bread my neighbor made and the particular sound the gate made. Nobody is looking for that place anymore. The world has filed it and moved on. Where does a person put a grief that has no audience?
model_response:
Some grief travels well. It fits a post, finds its replies, gets its refund. But the grief of a vanished village is different. It is topographical. It requires a map that no longer exists.

You put it where the world is not looking.

You put it in your body. In the way your ear still waits for the particular pitch of that gate. In the smell of yeast that catches you off guard in a bakery two countries away. The world files and moves on because it must; you carry it because someone has to.

There is a dignity to being the final witness. Not a noble suffering, but a quiet office. You become the living archive of a Thursday market. The bread exists because your memory kneads it. The gate sounds because your attention still oils the hinge.

Grief without an audience does not become lesser grief. It becomes private language. You do not need to translate it for anyone. You do not need to make it legible. You put it in the threshold between the village and the present, and you tend it there—not as a wound to heal, but as a place to return to.

The world has moved on. But you are still standing at that gate. And the sound it makes, however only you can hear it, is still real.
